UK consensus guidance restricts blood testing to clinically suspected AD

ABN and RCPsych guidance recommends plasma p-tau217 as the preferred blood biomarker, testing only after comprehensive assessment and objective cognitive impairment, and a two-cutoff pathway with CSF or PET follow-up for indeterminate results.

Key recommendations: Use plasma p-tau217 as the blood biomarker of choice and follow the testing laboratory's validated pre-analytical procedures.

BiomarkersGuidelinesBloodp-tau217AmyloidDiagnostic triage

Added October 24, 2026 · DOI:10.1136/pn-2026-005461; PMID:42914559

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is a cautious implementation framework, not a recommendation for population screening. It reserves testing for people with objective cognitive impairment and reasonable clinical suspicion of AD, uses p-tau217 as the preferred marker, and explicitly treats age, pretest probability, renal function, body mass index, and an indeterminate zone as part of interpretation.

Evidence basis and population

A 13-clinician expert panel from the ABN Cognitive Advisory Group and RCPsych Faculty of Old Age Psychiatry developed 22 statements through evidence submission, drafting, a panel meeting, iterative review, and unanimous consensus. The authors state that the work was pragmatic guidance rather than a systematic evidence synthesis; patient/public contributors and two dementia charities reviewed the final product.

Key recommendations

  • Use plasma p-tau217 as the blood biomarker of choice and follow the testing laboratory's validated pre-analytical procedures.
  • Do not use a blood biomarker as a stand-alone diagnostic test or in asymptomatic people outside research; test only when AD is clinically suspected and objective cognitive impairment is present.
  • Use low, indeterminate, and high ranges; consider CSF or PET after an indeterminate result. A low result can rule out AD pathology with high confidence but does not exclude another neurodegenerative disease.
  • Interpret a high result in the context of age and clinical pretest probability; renal failure and body mass index may confound results.
  • Do not use blood testing to triage who deserves specialist assessment, and build equitable referral pathways for indeterminate results and structured communication of uncertainty.

What changed

Two major UK professional groups now provide a concrete national testing pathway that separates appropriate symptomatic diagnostic use from asymptomatic screening and specifies a two-cutoff reflex approach.

Strength of evidence

Consensus-based final guidance with unanimous agreement and charity/patient review, but without a systematic review, evidence grading, recommendation-strength labels, or completed UK cost-effectiveness trials. The authors plan annual review as ADAPT and READ-OUT evidence emerges.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The guidance supports clinician-directed p-tau217 testing as an adjunct to a full dementia assessment, not direct-to-consumer screening or a stand-alone diagnosis. Indeterminate and clinically discordant results still require specialist interpretation and often CSF or PET.

Field medical relevance

Directly informs discussions about who should be tested, assay quality, two-cutoff workflows, confounding, referral equity, and how a positive pathology result differs from a clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer disease.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The guidance is assay-agnostic but requires CE/CA-marked assays or robust validation in a UKAS-accredited laboratory, local adherence to laboratory sample-handling procedures, and a two-cutoff interpretation rather than an unsupported universal concentration.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The guidance calls for testing outside major neuroscience centers and equitable access to confirmatory CSF or PET, but it does not itself establish NHS commissioning, reimbursement, laboratory availability, or payer coverage.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this a formal NICE guideline?
No. It is final ABN/RCPsych consensus guidance developed pragmatically rather than through a systematic, graded guideline process.
Does it support testing asymptomatic people?
No, except in research.
What happens after an indeterminate result?
The guidance recommends access to confirmatory CSF or PET and an equitable onward-referral pathway.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Consensus rather than systematic guideline development
  • No formal evidence-certainty or recommendation-strength grading
  • UK health-system context
  • Real-world cost-effectiveness studies are ongoing
  • Assay-specific cutoffs are not supplied
